title: Safeguarding adults at risk
blurb: Who counts as an adult at risk under the Care Act 2014, the types and signs of abuse, and how to raise a concern while respecting the adult's choices.
question: An 82-year-old patient with dementia attends with her son, who answers every question for her. She has unexplained bruises on her forearms, her dentures are dirty and loose, and while he is out of the room she says quietly that he 'looks after all my money now'. What should you notice, and what should you do?

teach.h: Who is an adult at risk?
teach.body: In England, the Care Act 2014 places safeguarding adults on a legal footing, with the local authority leading. An adult at risk is someone aged 18 or over who has needs for care and support, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and, because of those needs, can't protect themselves from it. Being old or disabled does not by itself make someone an adult at risk. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own adult protection laws and policies with the same aims.

teach.h: The Care Act test: all three apply

steps.label: Is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect
Can't protect themselves because of those needs

teach.h: Ten types of abuse (Care Act guidance)
head: Type
Example
rows: Controlling or violent partner or family
Taking money, pressure over wills or property
Abuse because of race, disability, religion etc.
Poor care across a care home or service
Care needs ignored, e.g. no help with dentures
Not caring for own hygiene, health or home

teach.h: Signs the dental team may see
teach.body: Unexplained bruises or injuries, especially to the face, mouth or arms; dirty, lost or ill-fitting dentures and poor oral hygiene in someone who relies on carers; weight loss; a patient who seems frightened of their companion, or a companion who won't let them speak alone; sudden money problems or a carer controlling payments; and repeated missed appointments. Domestic abuse often shows as facial injuries, so the dental team may be among the first to notice.

letters.sub: Support the person to make their own decisions
The least intrusive response for the risk
Support for those in greatest need
Work with communities and other services
Be open and transparent in what you do

teach.caption: These six principles come from the Care Act statutory guidance.

teach.body: Adults with mental capacity have the right to make their own decisions, even unwise ones. So, where possible, talk to the adult about your concern and what they want to happen ('making safeguarding personal'), and seek their consent before sharing. You can still share without consent if other people are at risk, a crime may have been committed, there is a serious risk to life, they are being coerced, or they lack capacity to decide (when you act in their best interests).

teach.h: Raising a concern about an adult

steps.label: Recognise
steps.sub: Notice signs or listen to a disclosure

steps.label: Respond
steps.sub: Make them safe; 999 if in immediate danger

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Facts, exact words, date, time, signed

steps.label: Report
steps.sub: Practice safeguarding lead, the same day

teach.body: Prevent is part of safeguarding. It aims to stop people being drawn into terrorism, often by spotting vulnerable people being groomed into extremist views. If something a patient or colleague says or does worries you in this way, treat it like any other safeguarding concern: record it and tell the safeguarding lead, who can seek advice and, if appropriate, refer to the multi-agency Channel programme.

teach.text: Old age, dementia or disability alone don't make someone an adult at risk: all three Care Act conditions must apply. And financial, organisational, discriminatory and self-neglect are ADULT categories; the four child categories are physical, emotional, sexual and neglect.

items: Care Act 2014: care and support needs + abuse or risk of it + can't protect self.
Ten types include financial, domestic, organisational, discriminatory, modern slavery and self-neglect.
Signs: unexplained injuries, neglected dentures and hygiene, fear of a companion, money being controlled.
Six principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, accountability.
Seek consent where the adult has capacity, but share without it when others are at risk or life is in danger.
Recognise, respond, record, report to the safeguarding lead, refer to adult social care.

summary: You can now apply the Care Act 2014 test for an adult at risk, name the ten types of abuse, spot signs in the dental setting, explain the six safeguarding principles, and raise a concern correctly while respecting the adult's right to make their own decisions.

A.q: A patient with dementia says her carer 'looks after all my money now' and she can no longer pay for her new denture. Which type of abuse might this indicate?
A.why: Someone controlling or taking an adult's money or property, especially with sudden inability to pay, may be financial or material abuse.

whyNot.0: Discriminatory abuse is abuse because of a protected characteristic such as race or disability.
whyNot.1: Organisational abuse is poor care across a whole service or care home.
whyNot.2: Self-neglect is a person not caring for themselves, not someone else taking their money.

A.q: Under the Care Act 2014, which statement describes an adult at risk?
options: Any adult over 65 attending for dental treatment
Anyone who is registered disabled or uses a wheelchair daily
Has care needs, faces abuse and can't protect themselves
Any adult who has missed two or more appointments
A.why: All three conditions must apply: care and support needs, abuse or risk of it, and inability to protect themselves because of those needs.

whyNot.0: Age alone doesn't make someone an adult at risk.
whyNot.1: Disability alone doesn't meet the test.
whyNot.3: Missed appointments may be a sign, but they don't define an adult at risk.

A.q: A care home resident arrives with very dirty dentures that look as if they haven't been removed for weeks. This most suggests:
A.why: Failing to meet basic care needs, such as help with denture hygiene, may be neglect, and could indicate wider poor care in the home.

whyNot.0: Modern slavery involves forced labour or trafficking.
whyNot.3: There's no indication the poor care is because of a protected characteristic.

B.q: An adult with full capacity discloses that her partner hits her, but asks you not to tell anyone. No children or others are at risk. What is the best approach?
options: Report it to the police straight away, without telling her first
Do nothing further, as she has capacity to decide
Discuss options with her and involve the safeguarding lead
Tell her partner that you know what is happening
B.why: Respect her choices, talk through support and options, and seek advice from the safeguarding lead, who will consider whether there's a reason to share without consent.

whyNot.0: Without a serious risk to life, a crime against others or risk to others, the adult's wishes should normally guide the response.
whyNot.1: Capacity doesn't mean doing nothing; she still needs support and the concern must be recorded and discussed.
whyNot.3: Confronting the partner could put her in greater danger.

B.q: Which of these is one of the six safeguarding principles in the Care Act guidance?
B.why: The six principles are empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability.

whyNot.1: Safeguarding is about protection, not punishment.
whyNot.2: Profit has nothing to do with safeguarding.
whyNot.3: Confidentiality matters, but it isn't a principle and can be overridden to protect people.

B.q: An elderly patient seems frightened of her son, who won't let her be seen alone. Who should you tell first?
options: The son, to hear his side
Her neighbours, to ask what they think
B.why: Record your observations and raise them with the practice safeguarding lead the same day.

whyNot.0: Telling the son could increase the risk to her.
whyNot.3: An adult at risk may be too frightened to complain; you must act on your concern.

C.q: Which local body leads adult safeguarding enquiries in England under the Care Act 2014?
C.why: The local authority (adult social care) leads safeguarding enquiries, working with partners such as health and the police.

whyNot.2: CQC regulates services; it doesn't lead individual safeguarding enquiries.
whyNot.3: The dentist raises concerns; they don't run safeguarding enquiries.

C.q: When may a concern about an adult be shared WITHOUT their consent?
options: Whenever any colleague asks about the patient
Only if the adult is aged over 80 years
When others are at risk or life is in danger
Never, under any circumstances at all
C.why: Information can be shared without consent where others are at risk, there's serious risk to life, a crime may have been committed, coercion is involved, or the adult lacks capacity.

whyNot.0: Curiosity is never a reason to share confidential information.
whyNot.1: Age is not a test for sharing without consent.
whyNot.3: There are clear situations where sharing without consent is justified.

C.q: A patient makes remarks suggesting he is being drawn into violent extremist views. How should this be handled?
options: Argue with him about his views
Ignore it, as it isn't really a dental matter
Record it and tell the safeguarding lead
C.why: Prevent is part of safeguarding. Record the concern and pass it to the safeguarding lead, who can seek advice and refer if appropriate.

whyNot.0: Arguing doesn't protect anyone and could escalate the situation.
whyNot.1: Safeguarding concerns apply whatever the setting.
whyNot.2: Going to the press breaches confidentiality and is inappropriate.

reteach.title: Three keys to the same lock
reteach.question: Imagine a lock that only opens when three keys turn together. How does that help you decide whether someone is an adult at risk under the Care Act?

blocks.body: Key one: the person has care and support needs, such as dementia. Key two: they're being abused or neglected, or are at risk of it. Key three: because of their needs, they can't protect themselves. If all three turn, the safeguarding 'lock' opens and the local authority has a duty to make enquiries. Your role is to spot the keys and tell the safeguarding lead, while listening to what the person wants.

blocks.text: An adult with capacity can make unwise choices. Support them, record, and seek advice, but don't override them unless others are at risk or life is in danger.

explain.body: An adult at risk has care and support needs, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and can't protect themselves because of those needs. All three must apply.

test.q: A fit, independent 70-year-old with no care needs is being sold an overpriced boiler by a doorstep trader. Under the Care Act, is she an adult at risk?
options: No, because scams are never a form of abuse
No, she has no care and support needs
test.why: Without care and support needs, the Care Act safeguarding test isn't met, although she may still need advice or help from other services.

whyNot.0: Age alone doesn't meet the test.
whyNot.1: Scams can be financial abuse; the issue here is the missing care-needs condition.
whyNot.2: The test needs all three conditions, not just a risk of harm.

explain.body: Physical, domestic, sexual, psychological, financial or material, modern slavery, discriminatory, organisational, neglect and acts of omission, and self-neglect.

test.q: Poor care practices affecting many residents across a care home are an example of:
test.why: Organisational (institutional) abuse is poor care or neglect built into how a service is run.

whyNot.0: Self-neglect is about an individual not caring for themselves.
whyNot.1: Discriminatory abuse is linked to protected characteristics.
whyNot.3: Psychological abuse involves threats, humiliation or control of an individual.

explain.body: Adults with capacity can make their own choices, even unwise ones. Talk to them and seek consent. Share without consent if others are at risk, life is in danger, a crime may have been committed, there is coercion, or they lack capacity (best interests).

test.q: An adult who lacks capacity is showing signs of neglect. On what basis can you share your concern?
options: Only if a family member agrees
test.why: When an adult lacks capacity to decide, you act in their best interests under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, which can include sharing concerns.

whyNot.0: They can't give valid consent if they lack capacity.
whyNot.2: Family agreement isn't required to safeguard someone.
whyNot.3: A court order isn't needed to raise a safeguarding concern.

explain.body: Recognise, respond (999 if in immediate danger), record the facts and exact words, report to the safeguarding lead the same day, who refers to adult social care.

test.q: After recognising signs that an adult may be being abused, and making sure they're safe, what comes next?
options: Record the facts and tell the lead
Wait to see if it happens again
Ask the patient to sign a statement
test.why: Record what you saw and heard accurately, then report to the safeguarding lead the same day.

whyNot.1: Confrontation can increase the risk to the adult.
whyNot.3: Taking formal statements isn't your role.
